question: What happens when you compile and execute a C++ program?

scenes.sub: From a text file to a running process: four tools, then the OS.
scenes.say: What actually happens between writing hello dot c p p and seeing Hello on the screen? Let's follow one file all the way.

scenes.head: Our file
scenes.say: It has an include, a macro, and main. Typing g plus plus hello dot c p p looks like one step. But four separate tools run, one after another.

scenes.head: Build: four stages
scenes.say: First, the preprocessor. It pastes in the full text of every include, and replaces macros like GREETING with their value. Then the compiler checks your syntax and types, and translates C plus plus into assembly. The assembler turns that assembly into machine code, called an object file. Finally, the linker joins your object files with library code, like the code behind cout, into one executable.

scenes.head: Stop at any stage yourself

panels.code:
g++ -E hello.cpp -o hello.i    // preprocess only
g++ -S hello.cpp -o hello.s    // stop after compiling
g++ -c hello.cpp -o hello.o    // stop after assembling
g++ hello.o -o hello           // link
./hello

scenes.say: You can stop at each stage yourself. Dash E stops after preprocessing. Dash S gives you the assembly. Dash c gives an object file. And without those flags, g plus plus links everything into a program. Then run it.

scenes.head: Why it matters: reading errors

output.text:
undefined reference to `add(int, int)'
collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status

scenes.say: Knowing the stages helps you read errors. This code compiles fine, because the compiler only needs to know that add exists. But the linker can't find add's body anywhere, so it fails with undefined reference. L D is the linker.

scenes.head: Run: the OS takes over
scenes.say: When you run it, the operating system's loader creates a process. It maps the machine code into the text segment, sets up globals in the data segment, and gives you a heap and a stack. Startup code constructs any global objects, then calls main. When main returns zero, that becomes the exit code, telling the shell the program succeeded.

lines: Preprocess → Compile → Assemble → Link. One command, four tools.
Type and syntax errors come from the compiler. “undefined reference” comes from the linker.
Run: the OS loads the program, sets up memory, calls main(). Its return value is the exit code.
scenes.say: Remember. Preprocess, compile, assemble, link. Type and syntax errors come from the compiler, and undefined reference comes from the linker. Running means the OS loads the program, sets up its memory, and calls main, whose return value becomes the exit code.
